questions.q: Why does this platform define cents_to_dollars() as a shared macro instead of writing the conversion inline in every model that needs it?
options: Inline SQL is not allowed inside dbt models
One shared definition means one place to get the divisor right, instead of three separate models each risking a different mistake
Macros execute faster than inline arithmetic in Snowflake
dbt requires every numeric conversion to be wrapped in a macro
questions.explain: A shared macro removes the risk of multiple models quietly disagreeing about how cents convert to dollars.

questions.q: What does the date_spine_days() macro in this lesson actually do?
options: It deletes rows outside a given date range
It wraps dbt_utils.date_spine with this platform's own simpler call signature, useful anywhere a mart needs one row per calendar day
It converts a date column into a string
It snapshots a table on a daily schedule
questions.explain: date_spine_days wraps the real dbt_utils.date_spine macro so every model doesn't have to re-derive its arguments from scratch.

questions.q: Why is payment_method_is_valid() useful in both a model's WHERE clause and a future custom test, per this lesson?
options: Because macros can only be called from tests, never from models
So the same definition of "valid payment method" can't drift between a model and the test checking it — one source of truth
Because WHERE clauses require a macro by dbt convention
It has no real use in a test, only in models
questions.explain: Reusing one macro in both places guarantees a model and its governing test can never quietly disagree about what counts as valid.

questions.q: How is a macro called from inside a model's SQL?
options: By importing it with a Python import statement
With {{ macro_name(...) }}, the same Jinja syntax used for built-in dbt functions like ref() and source()
By writing CALL macro_name() as a separate SQL statement
Macros cannot be called from models, only from other macros
questions.explain: {{ cents_to_dollars('amount') }} is called exactly like a built-in dbt function, because macros use the same Jinja templating mechanism.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call a shared macro library a governance tool, not just a convenience?
options: Because it requires ACCOUNTADMIN to create macros
Because a business rule like "valid payment methods" becomes a single, named, version-controlled definition instead of a value repeated inconsistently across files
Because macros are automatically tested by dbt with no extra configuration
Macros have no governance value in this lesson's framing
questions.explain: Centralizing a business rule in one macro means a future change to that rule is a one-line edit, not a search-and-replace across the whole project.
